screens.title: Managing Swap Space
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn what swap space is, when the Linux kernel uses it, and how to create and manage swap partitions and swap files. Think of swap as a fallback area on disk that holds memory pages the kernel can evict from R A M when the system is under memory pressure. Swap prevents out-of-memory crashes and supports features like hibernation, but because disks are much slower than R A M, relying on swap slows performance. We'll walk through both swap partition and swap file workflows: preparing the device or file, initializing with mkswap, activating with swapon, and making the change persistent in /etc/fstab. You will also learn how to monitor swap usage with free and swapon, and how to tune vm. swappiness to change how aggressively the kernel swaps. By the end you'll be able to add a temporary swap file, secure it with correct permissions, verify swap is active, and make it persist across reboots. This matters because correct swap setup avoids crashes, supports services that briefly spike memory, and gives you operational control over performance versus safety.

screens.title: What is swap space and why it exists
screens.narratorSegment: Swap space is disk-backed virtual memory the kernel uses to move less active pages out of R A M when physical memory is scarce. The key idea is simple: R A M is fast but limited. Swap gives the system additional addressable memory by storing inactive pages on disk. This prevents out-of-memory crashes and supports hibernation, where R A M contents are written to swap before power off. However, swap is orders of magnitude slower than R A M. That means while swap prevents immediate failure, heavy or frequent swapping—called thrashing—will slow the whole system because the kernel spends more time moving pages between R A M and disk. A useful mental model is a desk versus a filing cabinet: keep active work on the desk (R A M) for speed, move older documents to the cabinet (swap) to free space. When you explain swap, include both the protective role and the performance trade-off. A common misconception is that more swap always solves memory shortages; in reality, persistent heavy swap indicates you should add physical R A M or optimize workloads. Takeaway: swap is essential as a fallback but not a substitute for adequate R A M.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: Swap extends addressable memory but is slower; use it as a safety net, not a performance substitute.

content.html:
Definition
Swap space: disk-backed virtual memory
Protects against out-of-memory errors and enables hibernation, with significant performance trade-offs.

Swap stores inactive memory pages on disk when RAM fills. This lets the kernel free RAM for current tasks.

Because disk is much slower, moving pages in and out of swap impacts responsiveness.

Frequent swapping, or thrashing, indicates either insufficient RAM or poorly-tuned swappiness.

Key Takeaway

Swap is a safety net and hibernation target, not a replacement for adequate RAM.

Analogy & quick checks
Analogy: desk (RAM) vs filing cabinet (swap). Keep active items on the desk; move idle items to the cabinet to free workspace.
When to rely on swap: short spikes of memory use, hibernation support, and emergency fallback.
When not to rely on swap: continuous heavy usage. If swap is constantly used, consider adding RAM or adjusting workloads.
Check commands (use in terminal)
free -h
# shows memory and swap totals and usage

screens.title: Swap partition workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a swap partition follows a clear sequence of actions. First, create or identify a disk partition using fdisk or gdisk and set the partition type to swap (type 82 for MBR or 19 for GPT). This step ensures the partition is recognized as intended for swap by installers and tools. Next, initialize the partition as swap space with the mkswap command; mkswap writes appropriate metadata so the kernel can use the device as swap. Finally, activate the partition with swapon /dev/sdXN to immediately make the swap available. Verification is important: run swapon -s to list active swap devices and free -h to confirm the swap size appears in the system totals. A common mistake is forgetting to set the partition type or to run mkswap before swapon, which will result in an error. If you want persistence, add the partition device or UUID to /etc/fstab with the swap entry. Practicing these steps in order ensures reliable, repeatable swap partition setup. Swap partition workflow means create partition, set swap type, initialize with mkswap, activate with swapon, and verify with swapon -s and free.. In practical terms, partition, mark type, mkswap, and swapon. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process
Swap partition workflow
Step-wise commands and verification for a swap partition.
1
Create partition
Use fdisk or gdisk and set type to Linux swap (82) or 19 for GPT.
2
Initialize
Run sudo mkswap /dev/sdXN to prepare the partition.

Activate
Use sudo swapon /dev/sdXN, then verify with swapon -s.
Common mistake
Trying to swapon before running mkswap or using the wrong partition type will fail.

# create partition with fdisk or gdisk

swapon -s

screens.title: Swap file creation: safe, flexible, reversible
screens.narratorSegment: A swap file is a regular file on an existing filesystem that the kernel uses as swap. It is flexible because you can create or resize swap without repartitioning disks. The sequence is important: allocate a file with dd, set restrictive permissions to prevent other users from reading sensitive memory pages, initialize it with mkswap, and activate with swapon. For example, to create a 1GB swap file you use dd with a one-megabyte block size and a count of 1024. After creation, chmod 600 ensures only root can read or write the file. Then run sudo mkswap /swapfile and sudo swapon /swapfile. Verify with free -h and swapon -s. A common mistake is forgetting chmod 600; some versions of mkswap will refuse to initialize files with insecure permissions. Another is placing the swap file on a filesystem that doesn't support required operations. Swap files are ideal for temporary additional memory and quick fixes, but use fstab to make them persistent if needed. Swap file creation: safe, flexible, reversible means dd to allocate, chmod 600 to secure, mkswap to initialize, swapon to activate, then verify.. In practical terms, create a swap file with dd, secure it, initialize and activate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: dd to allocate, chmod 600 to secure, mkswap to initialize, swapon to activate, then verify.

content.html:
Definition
Swap file creation
Flexible alternative to a partition; create on any supported filesystem.

Use dd to allocate the file. Example below creates a 1GB file filled with zeros.

sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=1024

Set permissions to 600 to prevent unauthorized read access, then initialize and activate.

Code walkthrough
sudo dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=1024
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
free -h
swapon -s
Tip: If mkswap complains about permissions, double-check chmod 600. If the filesystem disallows required flags, consider a partition.
Key Takeaway

Swap files are quick to add and remove. Always secure with chmod 600 and verify activation.

screens.title: Persisting swap across reboots using /etc/fstab
screens.narratorSegment: To ensure swap is available after a reboot you must add the swap device or file to /etc/fstab. For a partition you can add either the device node, like /dev/sdb2, or the UUID, which is more robust if device names change. The fstab entry uses the none mount point and the swap filesystem type with defaults, example: /swapfile none swap defaults 0 0. After editing fstab, test the entries without rebooting by deactivating swap with sudo swapoff -a, then reactivating all fstab-listed swap with sudo swapon -a. This tests that your fstab line is valid and that the system will mount swap on boot. If swapon -a reports errors, check paths, UUIDs, permissions, and ensure mkswap has been run where required. A common oversight is adding the fstab entry but forgetting to create the swap file or run mkswap first, which will cause activation to fail during boot. Always verify with free -h and swapon -s after testing. Persisting swap across reboots using /etc/fstab means add swap entries to /etc/fstab and test with swapoff -a and swapon -a to ensure swap mounts on boot.. In practical terms, add swap entries for partitions or files and test them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process
Make swap persistent in /etc/fstab
Use device path or UUID for reliable boot-time activation.
fstab examples
# partition example
/dev/sdb2 none swap defaults 0 0

# swap file example
/swapfile none swap defaults 0 0

# recommended: use UUID
UUID=your_swap_uuid_here none swap defaults 0 0
After editing, test with: sudo swapoff -a && sudo swapon -a and then verify with free -h.
Testing & troubleshooting
  • swapoff -a deactivates all active swap.
  • swapon -a reads fstab and activates listed swap entries.
  • If swapon fails, check file path, permissions, device UUID, and that mkswap was run.
Common mistake: Adding an fstab entry before creating or initializing the swap file leads to boot-time errors; always test first.

screens.title: Swap partition vs swap file
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a swap partition and a swap file depends on your needs. A swap partition is stable, often slightly faster, and traditionally created during installation. It is a dedicated area with no filesystem overhead. A swap file is more flexible: you can add or resize it on a running system without repartitioning, which is ideal for quick fixes or temporary capacity. From a performance perspective, differences are usually small on modern kernels, but some filesystems or mount options can affect swap-file performance. Security-wise, swap files require strict permissions because they can contain memory contents; chmod 600 is essential. For persistence, both types can be listed in /etc/fstab, though partitions are commonly referenced by UUID. Common misconception: that swap files are always significantly worse; in many practical cases they perform acceptably and offer valuable flexibility. Choose a partition when stable, predictable swap is required; choose a file when you need easy resizing or quick deployment. Swap partition vs swap file means use partitions for stable, installer-managed swap and files for flexible, on-the-fly adjustments; secure files with permissions.. In practical terms, trade-offs: performance, flexibility, and manageability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Comparison
Partition vs File
Swap Partition • Dedicated device • Slightly simpler semantics • Often created at install
Swap File • Flexible and resizable • Create without repartitioning • Must set chmod 600
Consider filesystem behavior when using a swap file; some filesystems may need specific flags for best behavior. In most admin tasks, swap files provide fast operational flexibility.
Scenario card
Temporary: your VM spikes memory during a build. Create a 1GB swap file, activate it, and remove later.
Stable service: a database on bare metal with consistent memory needs may prefer a partition added at install time.
Key Takeaway

Balance flexibility and predictability: files = flexible; partitions = dedicated.

screens.title: Monitoring swap usage
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring swap usage is essential to understand memory behavior. The free -h command gives you a human-readable summary showing total, used and free memory and swap. swapon -s lists active swap devices and their used bytes. Both are quick checks after you add or remove swap. For example, free -h will show Mem and Swap lines with totals and available values so you can confirm the addition of your new swap file or partition. swapon -s prints a table with the filename, type, size, used, and priority. Use these outputs to verify that the system recognizes the swap and that its used column is reasonable. If swap usage steadily increases during normal load, you may be either underprovisioned in R A M or too aggressive with swappiness. Also use dmesg or journal logs to catch kernel messages about memory or swap errors. Regular monitoring after changes ensures that swap fixes the issue without introducing performance regressions. Monitoring swap usage means use free -h for a quick system summary and swapon -s for a device-level listing; check logs for related kernel messages.. In practical terms, use free and swapon -s to observe system behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Swappiness: what it controls and how to change it
screens.narratorSegment: Swappiness is a kernel parameter named vm. swappiness that controls how aggressively the kernel moves memory pages to swap. Its value ranges from 0 to 100. A higher value, such as the common default around 60 on many distributions, makes the kernel more likely to swap, freeing R A M for caches and prioritizing filesystem responsiveness. A low value, such as 10 or 0, tells the kernel to avoid swapping and keep applications in R A M as long as possible, which is often preferable for servers where application performance is critical. To check the current value read /proc/sys/vm/swappiness. To change swappiness temporarily use sudo sysctl vm. swappiness=10; this takes effect immediately but does not persist after reboot. To make the change persistent add vm. swappiness=10 to /etc/sysctl. conf and apply the file with sudo sysctl -p. A common misconception is thinking swappiness controls swap size: it only controls how eagerly swap is used, not how much swap exists. Tune swappiness based on observed swap use and performance. Swappiness: what it controls and how to change it means swappiness controls swapping aggressiveness; change temporarily with sysctl and persist in /etc/sysctl.conf.. In practical terms, adjust vm.swappiness to tune swapping behavior (0–100). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Definition
vm.swappiness
Range 0–100 controls how eagerly the kernel swaps inactive pages to disk.

Check current value: cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness

Temporary change: sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10

Persistent change: add vm.swappiness=10 to /etc/sysctl.conf and run sudo sysctl -p.

When to adjust

screens.title: Hands-on: Add a 1GB swap file (step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through adding a temporary 1GB swap file and making it persistent. First, allocate the file using dd: create a 1GB zero-filled file at /swapfile. Create a 1GB swap file

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to fix them
screens.narratorSegment: When working with swap, a few mistakes tend to repeat. First, incorrect permissions on a swap file cause mkswap or swapon to fail. The fix is chmod 600 on the swap file so only root can access it. Second, adding an fstab entry before creating or initializing the swap will fail during activation or at boot; always create and test the swap first, then add the fstab line and test with swapoff -a and swapon -a. Third, misreading free -h might lead you to think swap is heavily used; check the used column and correlate with observed slowness. If swap is in constant use, consider increasing physical R A M or reducing swappiness. Fourth, some filesystems or mount options can interfere with swap files; if a swap file cannot be used, consider creating a partition instead. For each issue, verify the resolution with swapon -s and free -h, and re-run the activation steps. Being methodical prevents failed boots and ensures predictable swap behavior. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn what swap space is, when the Linux kernel uses it, and how to create and manage swap partitions and swap files. Think of swap as a fallback area on disk that holds memory pages the kernel can evict from R A M when the system is under memory pressure. Swap prevents out-of-memory crashes and supports features like hibernation, but because disks are much slower than R A M, relying on swap slows performance. We'll walk through both swap partition and swap file workflows: preparing the device or file, initializing with mkswap, activating with swapon, and making the change persistent in /etc/fstab. You will also learn how to monitor swap usage with free and swapon, and how to tune vm. swappiness to change how aggressively the kernel swaps. By the end you'll be able to add a temporary swap file, secure it with correct permissions, verify swap is active, and make it persist across reboots. This matters because correct swap setup avoids crashes, supports services that briefly spike memory, and gives you operational control over performance versus safety.

These learning objectives are skills you will demonstrate by doing. First, you will explain swap's purpose and when the kernel moves memory to disk. That means being able to describe swapping, its role as virtual memory, and why it prevents out-of-memory crashes while impacting performance. Second, you will create and activate a dedicated swap partition: partition the disk, set the swap type, initialize with mkswap, and bring it online with swapon. Third, you will create and activate a swap file on an existing filesystem. This includes creating the file with dd, setting strict permissions, initializing, and activating it. Fourth, you will make swap persistent by adding the correct /etc/fstab entry and testing it with swapoff and swapon. For each objective you will also verify with free and swapon -s. These are practical, testable skills for system administration that keep services resilient under memory pressure and allow controlled, repeatable configuration across reboots.

This screen ties each objective to a concrete demonstration. For explaining swap purpose, you will compare R A M and swap using the desk versus filing cabinet analogy: R A M is the working desk, swap is a slower cabinet. Show when swapping happens by producing a small memory pressure and observing swap usage with free. To demonstrate creating a swap partition, you will create a partition, set its type to swap, run mkswap, then swapon and verify with swapon -s. For a swap file, you will run dd to allocate the file, chmod 600 to secure it, mkswap, then swapon, and confirm its presence in free -h. To persist configuration, you'll add the appropriate /etc/fstab line for the partition or file, run swapoff -a and swapon -a to test, and reboot optionally to confirm. Each demonstration includes verification steps so you can prove competency during an exam or in production.

Swap space is disk-backed virtual memory the kernel uses to move less active pages out of R A M when physical memory is scarce. The key idea is simple: R A M is fast but limited. Swap gives the system additional addressable memory by storing inactive pages on disk. This prevents out-of-memory crashes and supports hibernation, where R A M contents are written to swap before power off. However, swap is orders of magnitude slower than R A M. That means while swap prevents immediate failure, heavy or frequent swapping—called thrashing—will slow the whole system because the kernel spends more time moving pages between R A M and disk. A useful mental model is a desk versus a filing cabinet: keep active work on the desk (R A M) for speed, move older documents to the cabinet (swap) to free space. When you explain swap, include both the protective role and the performance trade-off. A common misconception is that more swap always solves memory shortages; in reality, persistent heavy swap indicates you should add physical R A M or optimize workloads. Takeaway: swap is essential as a fallback but not a substitute for adequate R A M.

Creating a swap partition follows a clear sequence of actions. First, create or identify a disk partition using fdisk or gdisk and set the partition type to swap (type 82 for MBR or 19 for GPT). This step ensures the partition is recognized as intended for swap by installers and tools. Next, initialize the partition as swap space with the mkswap command; mkswap writes appropriate metadata so the kernel can use the device as swap. Finally, activate the partition with swapon /dev/sdXN to immediately make the swap available. Verification is important: run swapon -s to list active swap devices and free -h to confirm the swap size appears in the system totals. A common mistake is forgetting to set the partition type or to run mkswap before swapon, which will result in an error. If you want persistence, add the partition device or UUID to /etc/fstab with the swap entry. Practicing these steps in order ensures reliable, repeatable swap partition setup. Swap partition workflow means create partition, set swap type, initialize with mkswap, activate with swapon, and verify with swapon -s and free.. In practical terms, partition, mark type, mkswap, and swapon. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A swap file is a regular file on an existing filesystem that the kernel uses as swap. It is flexible because you can create or resize swap without repartitioning disks. The sequence is important: allocate a file with dd, set restrictive permissions to prevent other users from reading sensitive memory pages, initialize it with mkswap, and activate with swapon. For example, to create a 1GB swap file you use dd with a one-megabyte block size and a count of 1024. After creation, chmod 600 ensures only root can read or write the file. Then run sudo mkswap /swapfile and sudo swapon /swapfile. Verify with free -h and swapon -s. A common mistake is forgetting chmod 600; some versions of mkswap will refuse to initialize files with insecure permissions. Another is placing the swap file on a filesystem that doesn't support required operations. Swap files are ideal for temporary additional memory and quick fixes, but use fstab to make them persistent if needed. Swap file creation: safe, flexible, reversible means dd to allocate, chmod 600 to secure, mkswap to initialize, swapon to activate, then verify.. In practical terms, create a swap file with dd, secure it, initialize and activate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

To ensure swap is available after a reboot you must add the swap device or file to /etc/fstab. For a partition you can add either the device node, like /dev/sdb2, or the UUID, which is more robust if device names change. The fstab entry uses the none mount point and the swap filesystem type with defaults, example: /swapfile none swap defaults 0 0. After editing fstab, test the entries without rebooting by deactivating swap with sudo swapoff -a, then reactivating all fstab-listed swap with sudo swapon -a. This tests that your fstab line is valid and that the system will mount swap on boot. If swapon -a reports errors, check paths, UUIDs, permissions, and ensure mkswap has been run where required. A common oversight is adding the fstab entry but forgetting to create the swap file or run mkswap first, which will cause activation to fail during boot. Always verify with free -h and swapon -s after testing. Persisting swap across reboots using /etc/fstab means add swap entries to /etc/fstab and test with swapoff -a and swapon -a to ensure swap mounts on boot.. In practical terms, add swap entries for partitions or files and test them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between a swap partition and a swap file depends on your needs. A swap partition is stable, often slightly faster, and traditionally created during installation. It is a dedicated area with no filesystem overhead. A swap file is more flexible: you can add or resize it on a running system without repartitioning, which is ideal for quick fixes or temporary capacity. From a performance perspective, differences are usually small on modern kernels, but some filesystems or mount options can affect swap-file performance. Security-wise, swap files require strict permissions because they can contain memory contents; chmod 600 is essential. For persistence, both types can be listed in /etc/fstab, though partitions are commonly referenced by UUID. Common misconception: that swap files are always significantly worse; in many practical cases they perform acceptably and offer valuable flexibility. Choose a partition when stable, predictable swap is required; choose a file when you need easy resizing or quick deployment. Swap partition vs swap file means use partitions for stable, installer-managed swap and files for flexible, on-the-fly adjustments; secure files with permissions.. In practical terms, trade-offs: performance, flexibility, and manageability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Monitoring swap usage is essential to understand memory behavior. The free -h command gives you a human-readable summary showing total, used and free memory and swap. swapon -s lists active swap devices and their used bytes. Both are quick checks after you add or remove swap. For example, free -h will show Mem and Swap lines with totals and available values so you can confirm the addition of your new swap file or partition. swapon -s prints a table with the filename, type, size, used, and priority. Use these outputs to verify that the system recognizes the swap and that its used column is reasonable. Swappiness is a kernel parameter named vm. swappiness that controls how aggressively the kernel moves memory pages to swap. Its value ranges from 0 to 100. A higher value, such as the common default around 60 on many distributions, makes the kernel more likely to swap, freeing R A M for caches and prioritizing filesystem responsiveness. A low value, such as 10 or 0, tells the kernel to avoid swapping and keep applications in R A M as long as possible, which is often preferable for servers where application performance is critical. To check the current value read /proc/sys/vm/swappiness. To change swappiness temporarily use sudo sysctl vm. swappiness=10; this takes effect immediately but does not persist after reboot. To make the change persistent add vm. swappiness=10 to /etc/sysctl. conf and apply the file with sudo sysctl -p. A common misconception is thinking swappiness controls swap size: it only controls how eagerly swap is used, not how much swap exists. Tune swappiness based on observed swap use and performance.
